titre: Sieyès (1789): The Third Estate Is “Everything,” but Asks for “Something”
accroche: Sieyès's slogan, “everything, nothing, something,” hides a very precise program, set out three times in the January 1789 text.
contenu_vulgarise:
“What is the Third Estate? Everything.” The formula is remembered as a battle cry: “everything,” “nothing.” But the text gives a third answer, a more modest one.

## Three Questions

*Qu'est-ce que le tiers état ?* (*What Is the Third Estate?*) is a pamphlet published by the Abbé Sieyès in January 1789, before the meeting of the Estates General. He announces his plan from the first pages: “We have three questions to ask ourselves.” What is the Third Estate? “Everything.” What has it been until now in the political order? “Nothing.” What does it ask? “To become something there.” The verb matters: the Third Estate does not ask to become everything, it asks to count.

## A Precise Count

The first answer rests on a calculation. Sieyès estimates that there are not two hundred thousand privileged people in the first two orders, against twenty-five to twenty-six million souls: further on, he contrasts the assembly of the Third Estate, which represents “twenty-five million men,” with the other two orders, whose powers come from only about two hundred thousand individuals. He concludes that the Third Estate “therefore embraces everything that belongs to the nation,” and that everything that is not the Third Estate cannot be regarded as being of the nation.

## Three Demands

The “something” has content. The Third Estate asks that its representatives be chosen from among the citizens who truly belong to it, that is, without any privilege; that it have a number of representatives equal to that of the other two orders together; and that votes be taken by head and not by order, without which equality of representation would be “perfectly illusory.” Sieyès presents these claims as a minimum: “The true intention of the Third Estate is to have in the Estates General an influence equal to that of the privileged. I repeat, can it ask for less?” He judges these three demands insufficient, moreover: “the more one considers this subject, the more one perceives the insufficiency of the three demands of the Third Estate.”

## The Shift

The radicalism lies in the rest of the text, not in the slogan. In the final chapters, Sieyès writes that the Third Estate must assemble apart, without joining with the nobility and the clergy: “The Third Estate alone, it will be said, cannot form the Estates General. Well! So much the better! It will make up a National Assembly.” The announced program is a claim to equality within the Estates General; the fallback hypothesis is an assembly without the other two orders.

One may ask which of the two stayed in collective memory, and why.

carte.punch: Sieyès answers “Everything” and “Nothing,” but the third answer is “something.”
carte.idee: In his pamphlet of January 1789, Sieyès asks three questions about the Third Estate. It is “everything,” has been “nothing,” and asks “to become something there”: as many representatives as the other two orders, voting by head.
carte.source_courte: Sieyès, What Is the Third Estate? (1789)

quiz.question: What is Sieyès's third answer to the question “What does the Third Estate ask?”
choix: That the king give up convening the Estates General before reforming the abuses of the kingdom
To become “something,” with as many deputies as the other two orders combined and voting by head
To abolish the monarchy and have a constituent assembly elected by universal suffrage of the citizens
To obtain the abolition of all taxes for peasants and artisans, to be paid by the privileged alone
quiz.explication: Sieyès answers “something” and details three demands: representatives without privilege, a number equal to that of the other orders together, voting by head. He asks neither for the end of the monarchy, nor for universal suffrage, nor for a tax cut.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What order of magnitude does Sieyès give for the privileged of the first two orders?
choix: About two million, one tenth of the nation
Fewer than twenty thousand, a handful of families
Fewer than two hundred thousand, against twenty-five to twenty-six million souls
About five hundred thousand, one inhabitant in fifty
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Sieyès counts fewer than two hundred thousand privileged people against twenty-five to twenty-six million souls: it is this calculation that grounds his “everything.”

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Sieyès answer to those who object that the Third Estate alone cannot form the Estates General?
choix: So much the better: it will make up a National Assembly
The Third Estate will first have to obtain the king's agreement to sit
It will have to unite with the nobility to form a joint chamber
The Third Estate will then give up its three demands
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Sieyès turns the objection around: if the Third Estate alone cannot form the Estates General, it will make up a National Assembly, without the nobility or the clergy.
